pull_request.title: Global: Define full-detector roadmap, agent roles and ODD realism assessment
pull_request.head: planning/full-detector-roadmap
pull_request.body:
## Summary

Expand the tracker-centred project into a technically credible, full-detector successor to ODD, with a reproducible DD4hep implementation and a whole-detector TDR as final deliverables. Establish the planning checkpoint before stage B architecture work starts on a separate branch.

- Define full-detector objectives, scope, realism criteria, the M0–M7 roadmap, subsystem work packages, interfaces, generation workflow and continuous TDR development.
- Record the user-directed completion of stage A for progression using ODD/ColliderML evidence; preserve the distinction between external evidence and locally unexecuted checks.
- Define the Project Responsible, System Architect, tracker/calorimeter/muon technicians, Software Engineer, Publication/Documentation Office, and independent Physics and Performance Validation roles.
- Add a revision-specific critical ODD assessment, ten prioritized gaps with closure evidence, source register, reading intake and static evidence inventories.
- Register the existing Overleaf TDR as `docs/tdr`, pinned to `7783ea3e3235c0fe9da641db3d303a6f211b3073`, and preserve curated session history.

## Review focus

Main documents: `PROJECT.md`, `docs/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md` (PLAN-NODD-001), and `docs/validation/ODD-realism-assessment.md` (M0-ODD-REALISM). ADR-001 gains verified source/license context and remains DRAFT; ADR-004/005 provide logging and reading context. No linked implementation issue, detector design sign-off, geometry change or stage B implementation is included.

## Validation

- 15 logging/documentation tests and 4 reference-download tests passed.
- 21 session records validated.
- Source IDs are unique; SHA-256 checks verified 20 local reference files and 77 upstream source files.
- TDR submodule checkout is clean; staged/unstaged whitespace checks passed.
- Earlier static assessment parsed 20 upstream XML files; this is not DD4hep construction or performance validation.

No DD4hep/Geant4/ACTS runtime checks or LaTeX build were performed. Reference PDFs, extraction caches and the upstream study checkout remain ignored local artifacts. Initializing the TDR submodule requires access to the Overleaf project; its contents are unchanged. Review/merge this checkpoint before beginning the separate stage B branch.

events.text:
I’ve made these objectives explicit in [PROJECT.md]([redacted] and the realism charter, and written the detailed [development plan]([redacted]

## 1. The destination

**Build a technically credible successor to ODD: a detector that could plausibly have been built, assessed through simulation and performance.**

That means:

- Preserve ODD’s broad character and its role in **TrackML → ODD → nODD**.
- Allow justified changes or complete rewrites of components and implementation.
- Give inherited components the same scrutiny as new ones.
- Cover active detectors, electronics, supports, cooling, services, magnetic fields and their interfaces.
- Deliver a reproducible DD4hep detector and a whole-detector **TDR**.
- Keep detailed engineering certification outside the present scope, while documenting assumptions that could affect simulation.
- Treat **nODD as a working name**.

## 2. Recommended approach

### A. Establish an unchanged ODD control — M0

First establish exactly what we are starting from.

Select the upstream revision, full-detector configuration, dependencies and required assets. Then characterize:

- Geometry, overlaps, dimensions, identifiers and sensitive coverage.
- Mass and directional material distributions.
- Magnetic fields throughout the detector.
- XML readouts versus digitization assumptions.
- Available Geant4 and reconstruction behavior.

**Deliverable:** a reproducible, reviewed baseline report with explicit limitations.

This gives us a control against which later changes can be understood.

### B. Define the whole detector before fixing its components — M1

Develop a coherent architecture covering:

- Intended research uses and performance observables.
- Broad layout, coverage and subsystem envelopes.
- Magnet concept and field representation.
- Shared supports, service corridors and transitions.
- Readout, identifiers and reconstruction interfaces.
- Which ODD features we retain, reconsider or replace.

**Deliverable:** an architecture proposal and shared interface register.

This should establish enough constraints to guide component work without prematurely freezing every dimension.

### C. Prove the method with representative assemblies — M1/M2

Start with the **RD53-class pixel module**, using ATLAS and CMS integration as separate evidence inputs.

Trace the complete assembly:

> chip and sensor → hybridization and flex → support and thermal path → power/data/cooling connections → material and response

In parallel, prepare a **calorimeter assembly** and a **muon chamber** case. These prevent our methods and generator from becoming pixel-specific.

Each case produces an evidence dossier, reviewed design, component inventory, validation specification and TDR section. Implementation follows the existing M0 and sign-off gates.

### D. Establish the specification-to-code workflow — M1/M2

Use those representative cases to decide what the detector specification must express:

- Materials, dimensions, transforms and repeated structures.
- Sensitive/passive boundaries.
- Segmentation and identifiers.
- Services and interfaces.
- Provenance and effective representations.

Then agree how it generates DD4hep factories and XML, including which reusable factories remain handwritten.

**Deliverable:** deterministic, inspectable generation with checks against both the specification and the resulting physical geometry.

### E. Develop subsystems with equal technical scrutiny — M3/M4/M5

| Workstream | Main realism questions |
|---|---|
| Pixels | Chip/sensor tiling, inactive regions, electronics, supports and services |
| Outer tracker | Strip geometry, stereo/paired sensors, hybrids and measurement model |
| Timing | Technology, coverage, integration and time response |
| Electromagnetic calorimetry | Sampling/cells, cassettes, cooling, readout and cracks |
| Hadronic calorimetry | Absorbers, active media, effective materials and containment |
| Muons | Chamber technology, gas/readout, stations and field requirements |
| Magnets/interaction region | Coil, cryostat, return concept, beam pipe and shielding |
| Common supports/services | Loads, routes, space, material and cross-system connections |
| Simulation/reconstruction | Response assumptions, operating conditions and performance |

**Magnet and service work starts during architecture.** It must influence active detector layouts.

Every subsystem progresses from small assemblies to repeated structures and integration, with its own reviewable evidence.

### F. Integrate and evaluate — M6

Use two distinct comparisons:

1. **Controlled comparison:** keep simulation and compatible reconstruction assumptions fixed to understand what geometry/material changes do.
2. **Best supported operation:** evaluate each detector with its justified response, calibration and reconstruction settings.

Progress from material probes and single particles to collisions and selected pile-up scenarios. Include transitions, cracks and forward regions.

A more realistic detector may perform worse than an idealized one. That is a result to explain, not a reason to remove physically justified material.

### G. Finalize the TDR and release — M7

Write the TDR throughout the project. Finalization should consolidate existing evidence.

It should cover architecture, components, services, fields, implementation, response, validation, performance, ODD comparisons, uncertainties and deferred engineering questions. Tie all results to a reproducible release, then settle the final name.

## 3. Agent organization

I recommend **one planning/integration coordinator with specialists activated for bounded tasks**.

The specialist roles would cover:

- Literature and provenance.
- Detector technologies and electronics.
- Supports, services and magnets.
- DD4hep and generation.
- Independent validation and reconstruction.
- TDR consistency.

Each assignment specifies inputs, allowed files, expected artifacts, dependencies and completion checks. Shared envelopes, materials and identifiers remain centrally coordinated.

Agents can research, propose, implement and challenge results. **Human domain reviewers retain design approval and acceptance.**

## 4. First work queue

The next useful jobs are:

1. Prepare the exact ODD baseline and environment proposal.
2. Extract the ATLAS/CMS RD53 module comparison.
3. Audit ODD’s material accounting and readout/digitization contracts.
4. Prepare bounded calorimeter, muon, timing and magnet evidence dossiers.
5. Use those findings to draft the successor architecture and TDR outline.

These evidence tasks can overlap baseline preparation.

**Yes—the structure is sound. The main missing function is independent physics/performance validation.** Most other gaps can be closed by clarifying responsibilities.

I’ve recorded **A as done for progression and B as active**, following your instruction. ColliderML provides substantial ODD simulation, digitization and reconstruction evidence; we can build on that. [ColliderML paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.15230v1)

## Recommended responsibilities

| Role | Main responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Project responsible** | Scientific objectives, requirements, priorities, tradeoffs and decisions requiring your input |
| **Project technician / systems architect** | Physical consistency: global layout, envelopes, interfaces, magnets/fields, common supports and services |
| **Tracker technician** | Pixels, strips, local electronics/supports/services; provisionally dedicated timing |
| **Calorimeter technician** | ECal and HCal technology, assemblies, electronics, cooling, gaps and response assumptions |
| **Muon technician** | Chambers, stations, readout, services, backgrounds and field requirements |
| **Project software engineer** | Specification/generation, DD4hep, simulation, reconstruction interfaces, CI and reproducibility |
| **Publication/documentation office** | TDR, source/claim traceability, terminology, figures and documentation consistency |

I would call the project technician a **systems architect**: its job includes resolving physical integration questions, beyond coordinating tasks.

## The loopholes to close

### 1. Who judges whether the detector performs credibly?

The software engineer should implement validation infrastructure, but should not be the sole judge of its results.

Add an **independent validation role**, reporting to the project responsible. It defines and challenges observables, assumptions, uncertainties and comparisons. This can be an occasional review agent rather than another permanent office.

### 2. Who owns everything between subsystems?

Explicitly assign common supports, cable routes, cooling distribution, power/data connections and material accounting to the systems architect.

Subsystem technicians own their local services **up to a named handoff**. Otherwise, each subsystem can look plausible while their combined services do not fit—or material gets counted twice.

### 3. Where do timing and forward infrastructure belong?

Three subsystem teams leave some ambiguity:

- Dedicated timing hardware: provisionally tracker.
- Calorimeter/muon timing response: respective subsystem.
- Beam pipe, shielding and forward interfaces: systems architect.
- Common time conventions: systems architect and software engineer.

### 4. Who owns detector response?

Split this deliberately:

- **Subsystem technician:** proposes physically credible response assumptions.
- **Software engineer:** implements them.
- **Validation reviewer:** challenges and checks them.
- **Project responsible:** owns the resulting scientific applicability statement.

This prevents thresholds, efficiencies, calibration or ageing assumptions becoming unnoticed software defaults.

### 5. Who can decide a cross-system change?

Distinguish the project responsible from the systems architect:

- Responsible: **what the detector must achieve**.
- Systems architect: **whether its physical arrangement is coherent**.
- Software engineer: **how that arrangement is represented and executed**.

For example, moving the solenoid requires a proposal covering calorimeter material, muon bending and reconstruction consequences—not an isolated magnet edit. Unresolved tradeoffs come to you; agents do not supply human sign-off.

### 6. Who verifies the documentation?

The publication office checks traceability and presentation. **Technical authors remain responsible for correctness.** Otherwise, polished TDR prose can turn an assumption into an apparently established fact.

## How I would start B

Give the roles a common first assignment:

1. **Project responsible:** architecture brief—use cases, recognizable ODD features and open decisions.
2. **Systems architect:** global layout/magnet alternatives and an interface-request template.
3. **Three subsystem technicians:** technology options, envelope needs, service demands and constraints using that template.
4. **Software engineer:** specification, readout, field and reconstruction contracts.
5. **Publication office:** TDR outline and evidence-coverage matrix.
6. **Validation reviewer:** criteria for comparing the combined architecture options.

Then consolidate these into **one coherent detector proposal** before detailed component implementation.

These are responsibility roles, not a requirement to keep eight agents running simultaneously. Each agent should receive bounded assignments and leave its decisions and handoffs in Git.
